entries.previousTitle: Decoy Effect – when a third option pushes you toward the second
entries.title: Decoy Effect – when an inferior option changes the comparison between better options
entries.description:
Decoy Effect is a context effect in which adding an inferior option can increase the choice share of another option. In the classic attraction-effect setup, the decoy is clearly worse than the target on important attributes, which can make the target easier to justify against a competitor.

Where can it show up?
- Pricing tables: a third plan can make one of the original plans look better by comparison.
- Product choice: an inferior model can change how price and quality trade-offs are evaluated between two stronger alternatives.
- Recommendations: adding or removing an option can change the relative appeal of the options that remain, even when their own features do not change.

A better check
- Compare the main options before and after the extra option is added.
- Ask whether the extra option is dominated by one alternative but not by the other.
- Remove the suspected decoy and see whether your preference between the remaining options changes.
- Compare the options on the attributes that matter to your goal, not only on the contrast created by the menu.
- Do not assume that every three-tier price table creates a decoy effect. The effect is well documented, but its size and even its direction depend on the choice set and context.
entries.reason: The legacy page called the Decoy Effect a marketing trick designed to push buyers toward a target. The literature supports a context-dependent choice effect, not a universal manipulation rule, and distinguishes several decoy configurations and related context effects.
